list.listitem: On examination, movement of a midline neck mass with deglutition and tongue protrusion suggests a thyroglossal duct cyst (TGDC). C
Confirm a normally functioning thyroid gland by palpation of the thyroid gland during physical examination and by a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level. C

Ultrasound (US), computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can provide information regarding the diagnosis and relationship of the cyst to the hyoid bone, helping to confirm the diagnosis, in addition to identifying normal orthotopic thyroid tissue. C
Patients with infected TGDC should receive antibiotic therapy and not undergo incision and drainage. Surgical excision should occur 6 weeks after the infection has been treated. C

Once diagnosed, the TGDC is best treated using the Sistrunk procedure to limit recurrence. C Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or chemical ablation are alternatives, although complete success rates are lower. C

background.definition: Thyroglossal duct cysts are the most common congenital cysts in the neck. They are cystic dilations of epithelial remnants of the thyroglossal duct tract, formed during the migration of the thyroid during embryogenesis. They present as midline neck masses at the level of the thyrohyoid membrane and are closely associated with the hyoid bone.

list.listitem: The exact incidence of TGDC is unclear. Many cystic remnants of the thyroglossal tract are never detected clinically; a post-mortem study of 200 adults found a 7% incidence of TGDC.
In one case series of midline neck masses in children evaluated by ultrasonography, almost half (48.4%) were diagnosed with a TGDC and 27.9% were diagnosed with a reactive lymph node.
There is no gender predilection.

Peak incidence occurs in the first three decades of life. The incidence of TDC has a bimodal distribution, 7.0 ± 4.2 years in children and 36.0 ± 18.0 years in adults, with similar incidence in children and adults.
Unknown

During its migration, the thyroid gland remains connected to the tongue by a narrow canal, the thyroglossal duct. The duct usually atrophies and disappears by week 10. Portions of the tract and remnants of thyroid tissue may persist, however, anywhere along this crescent-shaped descent from the tongue to the thyroid. Rarely a TGDC is found within the thyroid gland.
TGDC can arise anywhere where there has been failure of complete obliteration of the tract. Cystic dilations of this tract remnant result in the clinical presentation of a midline neck mass.

TGDC are most commonly located in the midline (75–82.6%) and at the level of the hyoid bone (44.4–75%), with 20–25% being suprahyoid, 15–50% anterior or posterior at the level of the hyoid bone, and 25–65% occurring infrahyoid. TGDC carcinomas occur in about 1%.
TGDC can extend into the oropharynx or laryngopharynx (21/250 cases in one series); in one case report, extension to the supraglottic area presented as a foreign-body sensation in the throat.
Most patients with a TGDC present with asymptomatic masses in the midline of the neck. On examination, movement of the neck mass with deglutition and tongue protrusion is suggestive for a TGDC. C
Confirm normal thyroid gland function by physical examination and TSH. C
If the thyroid is not palpable, ultrasonography or thyroid scanning (scintigraphy) may be valuable to document a normal thyroid gland. C
Ultrasound is the preferred imaging study given its adequate accuracy, ease of the administration, and lower cost when compared to MRI and CT scanning.
A CT scan can provide information regarding the relationship of the cyst to the hyoid bone, helping confirm the diagnosis, in addition to identifying normal orthotopic thyroid tissue. C

list.listitem: A TGDC usually presents with a midline upper neck mass that is cystic and causes no symptoms but may be slightly tender.
Patients, especially adults, can present with pain, dysphagia, dysphonia, and fistula formation.

Often the patient has or recently had an upper respiratory tract infection. There is no evidence of a cause-and-effect relationship; it may simply be that physicians are more likely to examine the cervical region at this time.
The mass is usually located at or below the level of the hyoid bone.

A midline neck mass that elevates with tongue protrusion and swallowing provides strong evidence of TGDC. The mass rises in swallowing because of the tract's close association with the hyoid bone, and it rises with tongue protrusion because of the connection to the base of the tongue.
Standard X-rays are nonspecific and offer little diagnostic value.

Ultrasound can provide information regarding the cystic pattern and pseudo-solid nature of a neck mass. It is also the method of choice to determine the presence of normal thyroid tissue because of its low cost and availability. Ultrasonography is less helpful in determining the exact pathologic characteristiscs of the lesion. However, in a retrospective study of children with midline neck masses, there was no association between preoperative US-based diagnoses and postoperative pathologic results.

The SIST (septae + irregular walls + solid components = thyroglossal) score components on US can help distinguish TGDC from other neck masses. In a retrospective study of 142 children of whom 83 had TGDCs and 59 had dermoid cysts, the SIST score had a sensitivity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value of 84%, 91%, and 81%, respectively. However, in another study of 45 pediatric patients with midline neck masses who underwent surgery, most patients had SIST scores of 0 and authors were unable to validate the score.

In a larger study of 47 children with TGDC and 25 with dermoid cysts treated surgically, the SIST score predicted the correct diagnosis 67% of the time; the SIST score criteria lacked specificity, however, and often lead to misclassification of TGDC as dermoid cyst. These authors developed a diagnostic algorithm using step-wise filtering of characteristics for septations, then depth to strap muscles, then cyst shape and lastly solid parts which correctly categorized cyst type in 100% of patients.

Thyroid scanning (scintigraphy) is used primarily preoperatively to demonstrate normal thyroid tissue. Radioisotope scanning should be only be used if the ultrasonography or thyroid function tests are abnormal.

The American College of Radiology recommends either CT neck with IV contrast or MRI without and with IV contrast as initial imaging for nonpulsatile neck masses in adults, adding US of the neck or MRI without IV contrast as usually appropriate for children.

CT is an excellent diagnostic tool for the evaluation of a neck mass. It provides information about the cyst and the cyst tract regarding size, localization, character, and relationship to surrounding structures. However, the radiation dose is high, especially for younger patients.

MRI can yield detailed information about a TGDC, and there is no associated radiation dose. In one study of 22 consecutive children with a midline cystic lesion at floor of mouth, diffusion-weighted MRI afforded excellent inter-observer agreement and was able to differentiate TGDC from dermoid cyst with an area under the curve of 0.94 and 0.96, sensitivity of 91% and 91%, specificity of 90% and 80%, negative predictive value of 90% and 88% and positive predictive value of 92% and 84% for both reviewers, respectively.

In one small retrospective study of 15 pediatric patients undergoing surgery for neck masses for whom more than one preoperative test was performed, sensitivity of US was 75% in diagnosis of TGDC while MRI sensitivity was 60% and CT was 82%. Ultrasound had the highest specificity at 80%.
To determine whether the patient is hypothyroid, a TSH level should be obtained.
Fine-needle aspiration can be used to diagnose TGDC or to exclude other diagnoses. In one case series of 22 children, though, diagnostic accuracy was limited.
Authors of a case report of a man with a rapidly growing TGDC found F-FDG PET/CT useful for evaluating the extent of malignant involvement in the TGDC squamous cell carcinoma.

Patients with infected cysts should receive antibiotic therapy and not undergo incision and drainage. Surgical excision should occur 6 weeks after the infection has been treated. C
Once diagnosed, the TGDC is best treated using the Sistrunk procedure to limit recurrence. C Fine-needle aspiration or chemical ablation are other treatment options. C
If the TGDC is infected, treatment with an antibiotic is indicated before planning surgical excision.
The antibiotics should cover upper airway pathogens. Examples include clindamycin, amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin), and ampicillin/sulbactam (Unasyn).
Fine-needle aspiration may be diagnostic and can help to decompress the cyst prior to surgical excision.

The surgical approach of choice for TGDC is the Sistrunk operation. This procedure includes excision of the midportion of the hyoid bone en bloc with the thyroglossal duct tract extending to the base of the tongue. Drain placement during a Sistrunk procedure does not appear to reduce rates of postoperative complications.
Recurrence rate is less than 6% after the Sistrunk procedure and 38% when an incomplete excision is performed.

In a single center retrospective study, patient age influenced surgical outcomes following Sistrunk procedures, with fewer adults and older children experiencing surgical failure compared to toddlers (3.6%, 16.7% and 38.9%, respectively).

A recent study revealed lower recurrence rates if the surgeons were fellowship-trained in pediatric otolaryngology vs surgeons with fellowship-training in pediatric surgery or pediatric plastic surgery (4% vs 30.1%, respectively).

In a retrospective chart review of 157 children who underwent surgery for TGDC, the modified Sistrunk procedure was similarly effective compared to the Sistrunk procedure, performed in 52 cases (33%), with similar rates of post-operative complications and recurrence rates (6% vs. 4%, respectively).
In a case series of 7 patients with recurrent TGDC, a wide anterior neck dissection technique was used for successful removal with no further recurrence over a 12-month average follow-up.

Authors of one study of 793 adults who underwent TGDC removal found infection rates to be higher following revision operations compared with primary operations (8.3% and 0.9%, respectively); 3% of patients experienced at least one post-operative complication. Complication rates appear to be higher among children. In a study of 91 children, mean age of 4.4 years, complications occurred in 24 children (26.4%). The most common complications were recurrence and wound infection (7.7% each), and hemorrhage and resection of thyroid cartilage were the most severe complications.
Successful endoscopic resection has been reported in several case series.

Patients with lingual TGDC need to have individualized management depending on their presentation and anatomic location. For cysts in close proximity to the hyoid, the Sistrunk's procedure is best; with a complete cyst excision sufficient for the rest.

US-guided fine-needle aspiration alone may be sufficient for patients with TGDCs. In one case series of 1075 patients with neck cysts, of whom 118 had TGDCs, 97% reported immediate shrinkage or improvement; however, 34% of those with TGDC had a recurrence.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 studies with 129 patients with TGDCs concluded that chemical ablation is an acceptable alternative to surgery, with a pooled success rate of 70% (95% CI 47%-86%). Options included were ethanol and OK-432, a lyophilized streptococcal preparation. The pooled success rate of ethanol ablation in this review was superior to OK-432 ablation, although with equivocal statistical significance (84% vs. 51%, p = 0.055). The pooled complication rate was low at 0.9% (95% CI 0.1%-5.8%). Repeat ethanol ablation had a lower pooled success rate of 47% (95% CI 24%-71%).

Authors of a systematic review of 32 studies of benign head and neck cystic masses treated primarily with sclerotherapy found a complete response rate of 60.5% with 11.6%. having no response to treatment. OK-432 was the most widely used agent, with a higher rate of complete response than that of ethanol (62.0% vs. 39.4%).

In a case series of 20 patients with TGDC, response rate to OK-432 was lower in those with multilocular cysts vs. unilocular cysts (9.1% vs. 44.4%, respectively). For those requiring surgery, there was no difference in operative time or bleeding for patients with or without prior sclerotherapy.

Surgical failures do occur. Areas of failure include misdiagnosis, inadequate hyoid bone resection, and persistent infra- or suprahyoid tract remnants; a complete Sistrunk procedure is advocated to limit recurrence.
Preoperative and postoperative infection is clearly associated with a statistically significant incidence of recurrent disease.

Postoperative hypothyroidism may occur, with patients progressing to myxedema in some cases, if an ectopic thyroid gland was present and excised with the Sistrunk procedure. These patients will require lifelong thyroxine replacement therapy.

Rarely, a cyst is found to contain thyroid carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinomas may arise in TGDC among older patients with an average age of 54 years. Cancer is usually diagnosed incidentally after the presumed TGDC has been removed. It is only noted histologically.

The Sistrunk procedure and removal of the TGDC are considered adequate surgical treatment of the carcinoma within a TGDC. A postoperative thyroid scan should be done to confirm that there is no carcinoma in the thyroid gland. If the scan reveals normal functioning thyroid, then no further surgery is indicated.

Authors of a systematic review found 164 reported cases of TGDC carcinoma; the vast majority were papillary cancer (92.1%). Most (68.3%) patients were female with a mean age at presentation of 39.5 years (9-83 years). Sistrunk procedure was conducted for nearly all patients and 61% underwent total thyroidectomy. Recurrence rate was 4.3% with a mean time to recurrence of 42.1 months from initial treatment; one patient died of TGDC carcinoma.
In one retrospective series of 15 cases of TGDC papillary carcinomas, BRAFV600E mutation positivity was associated with more locally advanced disease, necessitating radioactive iodine ablation.
Adult patients may have a more insidious presentation and are more apt to present with a symptom other than a mass or infection.

If not removed, as many as 50% of TGDC will become infected. In addition, although rare, malignant transformation and/or malignancy within the cyst can occur. In a case series of 26 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer in TGDCs, concomitant cancer in the thyroid and lymph node metastases was present in most cases.

Recurrence risk is about 5% following resection using the Sistrunk procedure. In a pediatric case series in Brussels, the recurrence rate was 11.5% (12/104 cases, 5 of whom were not treated with the Sistrunk procedure). Recurrence may be increased among patients with preoperative infection.

In a cross-sectional analysis of two surgical data-bases including 1532 (333 inpatient and 1199 outpatient) total cases of children (median age 5.16 years) with TGDC, there were no deaths, cases of sepsis or nerve injury. The adverse event rate was 4.4%, primarily from wound infections, unplanned reoperations and readmissions (2.6%, 2.2% and 2.0%, respectively), and was 2-fold higher among inpatients.

algorithm.title: Algorithm for the Management of Suspected TGDC.

cell.label: Suspected TGDC: Patient with midline neck mass
Suspicious for infection; tender, fluctuating in size, with dysphagia
Diagnostic workup including ultrasonography, thyroid scanning, and/or CT; and obtain TSH level
Surgical excision utilizing the Sistrunk procedure
Initiate antibiotic therapy guided toward common upper airway bacteria
